entry: English actor known for stage and screen work. Irons trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and began acting on stage in 1969. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for playing Claus von Bülow in *Reversal of Fortune* (1990), and a Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play for *The Real Thing* (1984). He also received a Primetime Emmy Award for *Elizabeth I* (2005). He voiced Scar in Disney's *The Lion King* (1994) and played Alfred Pennyworth in the DC Extended Universe films.

City (pop., 2017: 20,907) in the Jordan Valley of the West Bank, Palestine, and capital of the Jericho Governorate. Jericho is among the oldest cities in the world. Archaeologists have unearthed the remains of more than 20 successive settlements, and Jericho is the type site for the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B periods. Copious springs have attracted habitation for thousands of years. The West Bank was ruled by Jordan from 1950 and occupied by Israel in 1967. Administrative control of the city passed to the Palestinian Authority in 1994. In 2023 the archaeological site Tell es-Sultan was inscribed on the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage List, described as "the oldest fortified city in the world."

Early Christian priest, theologian and translator, known as Saint Jerome. He is best known for translating the Bible into Latin, a version known as the [[Vulgate]] that was commissioned by Pope Damasus I. Earlier Latin translations had relied on the [[Septuagint]], while Jerome attempted to base his Old Testament translation on a Hebrew version. He also wrote commentaries on the whole Bible, along with polemical and historical essays. His teachings on Christian moral life, especially in Rome, often focused on women. Jerome is one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers, with [[Ambrose]], [[Augustine of Hippo]] and Pope Gregory the Great. He is a saint in the [[Catholic Church]], the Eastern Orthodox Church and the Anglican Communion, and his feast day is 30 September.

American country and [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]] pianist, singer and songwriter, nicknamed "The Killer." Lewis made his first recordings in 1952 and became a pioneer of rock and roll and rockabilly. His 1957 hit "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" brought him worldwide fame, followed by "Great Balls of Fire." His career faltered after his marriage to Myra Gale Brown, his 13-year-old cousin. He had numerous country hits in the late 1960s and 1970s, including "Me and Bobby McGee." He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1986.

American comedian, actor and filmmaker, known as "The King of Comedy." Lewis rose to prominence in 1946 with singer [[Dean Martin]] as Martin and Lewis, making 16 buddy-comedy films before their split in 1956. He then appeared in 35 motion pictures from 1957 to 1984. As national chairman of the Muscular Dystrophy Association, he hosted its annual Labor Day telethon, which raised $2.45 billion for the organization from its 1966 inception to 2010. He received two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]], and France awarded him the Legion of Honor.

American former football wide receiver. Rice played 20 seasons in the [[National Football League|NFL]], winning three [[Super Bowl]] titles with the San Francisco 49ers. He is the career leader among wide receivers in receptions, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns, and he is widely regarded as the greatest wide receiver of all time. He was selected to the Pro Bowl 13 times and inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2010.

American stand-up comedian, actor and writer, known for observational comedy. He played a fictionalized version of himself in the NBC sitcom *Seinfeld* (1989–1998), which he co-created and wrote with [[Larry David]]. He earned a Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Musical or Comedy. Later he created the web series *Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee* (2012–2019), which earned him three Webby Awards, and co-wrote the animated film *Bee Movie* (2007). He has released four stand-up specials.

American broadcaster, television host and politician. He hosted the tabloid talk show *The Jerry Springer Show* from 1991 to 2018. The show was a commercial success, and Springer is noted as a pioneer of "trash TV." He began in politics as an adviser to [[Robert F. Kennedy]]'s 1968 presidential campaign and later served as mayor of [[Cincinnati]] from 1977 to 1978. He also hosted the courtroom show *Judge Jerry* and the talent show *America's Got Talent*. He died of [[Pancreatic cancer]].

Self-governing British Crown Dependency in the English Channel (pop., 2021: 103,267). The largest of the [[Channel Islands]], it lies about 14 miles off the Cotentin Peninsula of northwestern France. Historically part of the Duchy of [[Normandy]], it remained loyal to the English Crown but never became part of the Kingdom of England. German forces occupied the island during World War II until May 9, 1945. Jersey is a parliamentary democracy under a constitutional monarchy, with its own legal and financial systems, but it is not part of the [[United Kingdom]]. The economy centers on financial services, with agriculture and tourism.

American civil rights activist, Baptist minister and politician. A protégé of [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] in the civil rights movement, he founded organizations that later merged into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition. He finished third for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and was runner-up in 1988. From 1991 to 1997 he served as a shadow senator for the District of Columbia, and from 1992 to 2000 he hosted a program on [[CNN]]. A critic of police brutality and conservative policies, he was an early supporter of LGBTQ rights.

American outlaw and leader of the James–Younger Gang. During the [[American Civil War]], he and his brother Frank joined pro-Confederate guerrillas in Missouri and Kansas. Afterward the brothers robbed banks, stagecoaches and trains across the Midwest, gaining national fame. The gang's attempted robbery of a bank in Northfield, Minnesota, in 1876 led to the capture or death of several members. Robert Ford, a new recruit hoping for a reward, shot and killed James. Scholars describe the popular image of James as a [[Robin Hood]] figure as romantic revisionism, since there is no evidence that the gang shared its loot.

American track and field athlete. At the 1936 Summer Olympics in [[Berlin]] he won four gold medals, in the 100 meters, long jump, 200 meters and 4 × 100-meter relay. He set Olympic records in each of his three individual events, and ESPN credited him with "single-handedly crushing [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]]'s myth of Aryan supremacy." Earlier, at the 1935 Big Ten Championships, he won four events, set five world records and tied another in less than an hour. Owens returned to a United States marked by segregation, where he lacked scholarships or professional leagues and earned money in exhibition races against horses and dogs. In a 1950 Associated Press poll, he was voted the greatest track and field athlete of the first half of the century.

American actress and businesswoman. She rose to prominence at 19 in the television series *Dark Angel* (2000–2002), for which she received a Golden Globe nomination. Her films include *Fantastic Four* (2005), *Sin City* (2005) and *Valentine's Day* (2010). In 2011 she co-founded the Honest Company, a consumer goods firm selling baby, personal and household products. It was valued at roughly $550 million in February 2022.

American actress and photographer. Lange won Academy Awards for Best Supporting Actress for *Tootsie* (1982) and for Best Actress for *Blue Sky* (1994), in which she played a bipolar housewife. She won a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play for the 2016 Broadway revival of *Long Day's Journey into Night*. She won Primetime Emmy Awards for *Grey Gardens* (2009) and for the first and third seasons of *American Horror Story*. Lange has published five books of photography and is a Goodwill Ambassador for [[UNICEF]].

Catholic religious order for men, formally the Society of Jesus. Founded in 1540 by [[Ignatius of Loyola]] and six companions with papal approval, it is the largest Catholic religious male order and is headquartered in [[Rome]]. Jesuits have played a significant role in education and charity and are active in 112 countries. Jesuit missionaries spread across the world from the 16th to the 18th century, and the order has long been controversial. The Catholic Church expelled Jesuits from most European countries beginning in 1759, and Pope Clement XIV suppressed the order in 1773. The Church lifted the suppression in 1814.

Sung-through rock opera with music by [[Andrew Lloyd Webber]] and lyrics by Tim Rice. Loosely based on the Gospel accounts of the Passion, it centers on [[Judas Iscariot]], who is disillusioned with Jesus's ministry. The score was released as a 1970 concept album before its Broadway debut in 1971. The London production ran from 1972 to 1980 and held the record for longest-running West End musical until 1989, when [[Cats (musical)|Cats]] overtook it. Some religious groups objected to its sympathetic portrayal of Judas and its questioning of Jesus's divinity.

Martial artist, actor and philanthropist. A wushu champion before his film career, he starred in *Shaolin Temple* (1982) and became known for portraying the folk hero Wong Fei-hung in the *Once Upon a Time in China* series (1991–1993). After moving to Hollywood in the late 1990s, he starred in films including *Romeo Must Die* (2000) and *Hero* (2002). He is regarded as one of the two biggest names in martial arts cinema, alongside [[Jackie Chan]]. He founded the One Foundation in 2007, and *Time* magazine named him one of the 100 most influential people in 2010.

[[Fixed-wing aircraft|Fixed-wing]] aircraft propelled by one or more [[Jet engine|jet engines]]. Most jets fly at high speeds, either supersonic or just below the speed of sound, and typically cruise around Mach 0.8 at altitudes of 10,000–15,000 m, where jet engines operate most efficiently. Frank Whittle in England and Hans von Ohain in Germany developed the turbojet independently, Whittle from 1928 and von Ohain in the early 1930s. The Heinkel He 178 made the first flight of a turbojet aircraft on August 27, 1939. The Messerschmitt Me 262 entered service in 1944 as the first operational jet fighter, and up to 1,400 were produced. After World War II, jets became central to commercial aviation, and the [[Boeing 707]], which debuted in 1958, made transatlantic flights possible in hours rather than days.

Reaction engine that produces thrust by expelling a fast-moving jet of heated gas, usually air. Air-breathing jet engines, including turbojets, [[Turbofan|turbofans]], ramjets and scramjets, are internal combustion engines. Typically they have a rotating compressor powered by a turbine, with leftover power providing thrust through a nozzle, a process known as the Brayton thermodynamic cycle. Early jets used relatively inefficient turbojets for subsonic flight, so most modern subsonic jet aircraft use high-bypass turbofans, which give higher speed and greater fuel efficiency than propeller engines over long distances. Ramjets and scramjets instead use the ram effect of the vehicle's speed rather than a mechanical compressor. Thrust in a typical jetliner engine grew from 5,000 lbf (22 kN) in the 1950s to 115,000 lbf (510 kN) in the 1990s.

Fast-flowing, narrow air current in the atmosphere. The main terrestrial jet streams are westerly winds near the tropopause, flowing west to east around the globe. Each hemisphere has a polar jet, typically traveling at about 110 mph (180 km/h) at around 30,000 ft (9.1 km), and a weaker subtropical jet lies closer to the equator. The [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation]] affects their location, which in turn affects weather over the tropical Pacific Ocean. Meteorologists use jet stream positions in weather forecasting, and airlines use them to reduce flight times and fuel consumption. During World War II, Japan used the jet stream to carry Fu-Go balloon bombs across the Pacific to North America. Jet streams have also been detected on Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Federal subject of Russia in the Far East, with its administrative center at Birobidzhan. Designated by a Soviet decree in 1928 and established in 1934, it was intended as a Jewish autonomous region along the [[Trans-Siberian Railway]]. The Jewish population peaked at around 46,000–50,000 in the late 1940s, about 25% of the total, but its share declined steadily, especially after emigration to [[Israel]] in the 1990s. The 2021 Russian census recorded 837 ethnic Jews, or 0.6%. The region is one of two officially Jewish jurisdictions in the world, the other being Israel, and Yiddish is a recognized minority language.

History of the [[Jews]], from the Israelite kingdoms of the Iron Age to the present. The Assyrian and Babylonian captivities are regarded as the start of the Jewish diaspora. The Jewish–Roman wars of the 1st and 2nd centuries destroyed [[Jerusalem]] and the Second Temple and expelled many Jews. The Mishnah and the [[Talmud]] were composed in the following centuries, and diaspora communities coalesced into the *Ashkenazim*, *Sephardim* and *Mizrahim*. In the 19th century, pogroms triggered a mass exodus of more than two million Jews to the United States between 1881 and 1924, and the Zionist movement was officially founded in 1897. In the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], approximately six million Jews were murdered. On May 14, 1948, [[David Ben-Gurion]] declared the State of [[Israel]].

Literary works written by Jews on Jewish themes, in Jewish languages, or in any language by Jewish writers. Ancient Jewish literature includes [[Bible|biblical]] and rabbinic literature. Medieval works include philosophical, mystical and ethical writing, history, fiction and poetry. Medieval Hebrew poetry was influenced by the style of poets from [[Al-Andalus]], and Solomon ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi were prominent poets. Medieval Hebrew fables such as *Mishlei Shu'alim* ("Fox Fables") resemble [[Aesop's Fables|Aesop's fables]]. Modern Jewish literature emerged from the *Haskalah* and broke with religious tradition, and it contributed to many national literatures. It includes Yiddish, Ladino, Hebrew (especially Israeli) and Jewish American literature. Nobel Prize recipients include Shmuel Yosef Agnon, [[Saul Bellow]] and Isaac Bashevis Singer.

Ethnoreligious group and nation originating in the [[Israelites]] of ancient Israel and Judah. Judaism is its traditional religion, though many ethnic Jews do not practice it. Diaspora communities coalesced into three major ethnic subdivisions: the *Ashkenazim* of Central and Eastern Europe, the *Sephardim* of the [[Iberian Peninsula]] and later North Africa, and the *Mizrahim* of Asia and sometimes North Africa. Before World War II, the global Jewish population peaked at 16.7 million. Approximately six million Jews were murdered in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. As of 2021, an estimated 15.2 million Jews lived in the world, and today over 85% live in Israel or the United States. Jews have contributed significantly to science, philosophy, literature, governance and the arts.

Landlocked state in eastern India (pop., 2011: 32,988,134). Its name means "land of forests," and [[Ranchi]] is its capital. Formed in 2000 from southern [[Bihar]], it is the 15th largest state by area. Jharkhand accounts for more than 40% of India's mineral production, including coal, iron ore, copper and uranium, yet 39.1% of its population lives below the poverty line. Tribal communities such as the Santhal, Oraon and Munda form about 26% of the population.
